newsitem.title: IRAN: Poll shows Iran speaker set to win presidency.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows Iran speaker set to win presidency.

text.p: Iranian authorities on Tuesday said 280 people had been arrested in the capital for electoral offences, and warned against further violations in the Islamic republic's presidential campaign.

As they did so, a rare public opinion poll showed parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri holding a big lead in the run-up to Friday's polls, wide enough to ensure him overall victory on the first round.

In only the second poll of the 12-day election campaign, the newspaper Akhbar said 54.63 percent of respondents said they would vote for Nateq-Nouri and 37.42 percent for his main opponent Mohammad Khatami.
Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri got 4.70 percent and Reza Zaverei 1.29 percent. The other 1.96 percent were undecided.
Akhbar quoted pollster Jamshid Majidi as saying Nateq-Nouri's lead was considerable and it would be difficult to narrow the gap.

Tehran police chief Brigadier-General Youssef Reza Abolfathi told local media some 280 people had been detained up to Sunday for electorial violations. He did not specify them, but campaign posters plastered on city walls have been defaced and rumours have been spread about what life would be like under this or that candidate.

One rumour, for example, said women would be forced to wear the chador, an all-enveloping black veil, rather than a headscarf and a long coat over trousers, if the conservative Nateq-Nouri were elected.

The powerful Guardian Council, which selected the four presidential candidates from a field of 238 based on their loyalty to the Islamic government, said any violations of election rules must be countered indiscriminately.

"You are responsible for healthy elections," Ayatollah Ahmad Janati, secretary of the 12-man body of clerics and lawyers, told bodies set up by the council to oversee Friday's poll to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
Nateq-Nouri warned against election publicity turning into a smear campaign, suggesting that centrists close to Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who support Khatami were behind it.
Some Khatami supporters express concerns over conservative officials using their influence to ensure a Nateq-Nouri victory.
Rafsanjani, who has not publicly backed Khatami, warned officials on Friday about abuse of power to help any candidate and said vote-rigging would be an unforgivable treason.
Khatami, like Nateq-Nouri a Shi'ite cleric, has often come under attack during the campaign for being soft on Islamic values because of his reputation as a tolerant politician.

Forced to resign because of his relatively liberal views in 1992 after serving 10 years as culture minister, Khatami has gained wide support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear stricter Islamic rules regulating everyday life and freedom of expression if Nateq-Nouri wins.

Nateq-Nouri is backed by key clerical groups and is close to the bazaaris -- Iran's traditional merchant class of traders. His campaign has been boosted by remarks by Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who stopped short of openly backing him but urged clergymen to actively help voters make up their minds.
Some 33 million Iranians are eligible to vote. Campaigning is due to end on Wednesday night, allowing one day for reflection before voting.
An absolute majority of more than 50 percent of the vote is required for election. If no candidate wins sufficient votes on Friday there will be a run-off between the top two.

Akhbar newspaper said its poll was conducted in every Iranian province in three stages during April and May. It did not give the number of those questioned but said 47 percent of the poll sample lived in rural areas and the rest in cities.

The only previous poll, in Tehran Times on May 7, gave Nateq-Nouri 40.8 percent support, Khatami 33.8 percent and Reyshahri 8.2 percent. The remaining 17.2 percent chose other, unspecified candidates, were undecided or did not respond.

"Rafsanjani was speaker before he became president so Nateq-Nouri is almost designated to take over," said one of the few Western diplomats left in Tehran after Iran's row with the European Union over allegations of complicity in political assassinations of Kurdish dissidents in Germany.
"Nothing happens in Iran by chance," the diplomat said.
The presidency is Iran's highest office after that of the supreme spiritual leader, who has absolute power over all state institutions.
